Name: knowledge_type_geometry
Title: Do Different Kinds of Knowledge Live in Different Places? A Comparative Geometry of Factual, Conceptual, Relational, and Procedural Recall in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The four knowledge types the LLM community routinely conflates—factual (entity-attribute), conceptual (category/definitional), relational (compositional links between entities), and procedural (how-to/step-sequences)—are stored and retrieved by mechanistically distinguishable substrates: factual recall is localized in mid-layer MLP lookups, conceptual/relational recall is distributed across attention-mediated composition, and procedural recall is a late-layer serial routine. We hypothesize a single, type-agnostic probing+patching pipeline can reveal a reproducible 'localization spectrum' across types, and that this spectrum predicts (a) where editing works, (b) how robust recall is to paraphrase, and (c) when stored knowledge fails to surface.
Related Work: Geva et al. (2023) and Fierro et al. (2024) mechanistically dissect factual (subject-attribute) recall as MLP-enrichment + attention-extraction. Hase et al. (2023) show localization does not predict editability. Hochman et al. (2026) show factual retrieval is redundant/distributed/non-contiguous. Bahador (2025) offers a proof-of-concept that definitional knowledge is more localized than associative reasoning in fine-tuned GPT-2. Yu et al. (2023) study fact-vs-context competition. All of this work focuses almost exclusively on FACTUAL recall or on a single ad-hoc contrast; no prior work uses one unified pipeline to compare factual, conceptual, relational, AND procedural knowledge on matched queries, nor derives a quantitative 'localization spectrum' across types and links it to editability, paraphrase-robustness, and the knowing-but-not-answering gap. Our contribution is the first controlled cross-type comparative mechanistic study with matched query sets.
Abstract: Mechanistic studies of knowledge in language models have almost entirely targeted a single kind of knowledge—factual subject-attribute associations—leaving open whether the widely-invoked distinction between factual, conceptual, relational, and procedural knowledge corresponds to anything real inside the model. We ask a simple question: do different knowledge types occupy different internal substrates, and can we measure this on a common footing? We construct a matched benchmark in which the same underlying entities appear in four query forms—factual ('Paris is the capital of __'), conceptual ('A capital is a city that __'/category membership), relational ('The capital of the country bordering X is __'), and procedural ('To find a country's capital, first __')—so that surface form is controlled while knowledge type varies. We apply a single pipeline—layer-wise logit lens, linear probes, causal activation patching, and attention-knockout—to quantify, for each type: (1) a localization score (how few contiguous layers/components suffice for recovery), (2) an MLP-vs-attention reliance ratio, (3) the layer depth of peak information, and (4) paraphrase-invariance of the recovered mechanism. We hypothesize a reproducible localization spectrum: factual → most localized/MLP-driven/mid-layer; conceptual and relational → more distributed/attention-driven; procedural → latest-layer, serial. We then test whether a type's position on this spectrum predicts (a) success of ROME-style weight editing, (b) robustness to paraphrase and distractors, and (c) the frequency of stored-but-unretrieved failures. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama at multiple scales. This yields the first controlled comparative geometry of knowledge types and actionable predictions for editing and retrieval reliability.
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: Build ~4k base facts (from CounterFact/T-REx/world-capitals-style relations) and instantiate each in 4 matched query types (factual, conceptual, relational 2-hop, procedural step-sequence), each with 4 paraphrases and a distractor-context variant. Verify baseline accuracy per type so we only analyze items the model gets right (controlling for 'does it know'). 2) LOCALIZATION MEASUREMENT: For each type, run (i) logit lens per layer at the answer position, (ii) trained per-layer linear probes predicting the answer token, (iii) causal activation patching (clean vs corrupted subject/relation) to compute per-layer/component recovery, and (iv) attention-knockout to measure attention vs MLP contribution. Define quantitative metrics: LocalizationScore = 1 - (min #contiguous layers to recover 90% of clean logit diff)/depth; MLP-Attention reliance ratio from ablation deltas; PeakLayerDepth (normalized); MechanismParaphraseInvariance = correlation of per-layer patching profiles across paraphrases. 3) SPECTRUM TEST: Statistically compare metrics across the 4 types (mixed-effects model with random effects for entity and model). Predicted ordering: factual most localized/MLP/mid-layer; conceptual+relational distributed/attention; procedural latest-layer. Report effect sizes and significance. 4) EDITABILITY LINK: Apply ROME/MEMIT-style edits per type; measure edit success, generalization to paraphrases, and specificity. Test hypothesis that LocalizationScore correlates with edit success and specificity across types. 5) RETRIEVAL-GAP LINK: For each type, measure the rate of stored-but-unretrieved cases (answer decodable in mid layers via probe but not produced) and test whether more-distributed types have higher such rates. 6) GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (1B/2.8B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B) to check whether the spectrum ordering is scale/family invariant. METRICS: LocalizationScore, MLP/attn ratio, PeakLayerDepth, ParaphraseInvariance, edit success/specificity, retrieval-gap rate, cross-model rank correlation of the spectrum.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The four knowledge types may be entangled—relational queries include reasoning that is not pure retrieval; we mitigate by verifying single-hop storage of constituent facts and analyzing only correctly-answered items. 2) Matched-query construction may introduce surface-form confounds (procedural prompts are longer); we control by matching token length where possible and by including paraphrase sets. 3) Linear-probe decodability may be an artifact rather than causal 'knowledge'; we require causal patching corroboration for all localization claims. 4) Localization-editing links may be weak given Hase et al.'s known dissociation—this is itself an informative outcome, and we frame editability as one of several downstream tests, not the core claim. 5) The predicted spectrum ordering may not hold cleanly; a graded or model-dependent spectrum is still a publishable, informative result. 6) Procedural knowledge is hardest to operationalize as a single-token answer; we restrict to short procedural completions with a well-defined next-step token.
